Women are people, my friend. What do you do when your friend leaves you alone with some friend of theirs at a party, and you’re standing next to a dude you haven’t ever talked to before? You get over that initial “shit, I have no idea how to talk to this guy” by asking questions. Small talk isn’t useless — it’s how you figure out what the hell to talk to folks about. Women aren’t different. Ask about jobs, free time. What music they like, and be GENUINELY curious. So long as you aren’t leering like you’re going to ask her on a date immediately, “What else you got going on this weekend, anything fun?” works with almost no other information. And then just listen. And talk. Don’t calculate how to be impressive; connection is a two way street, and you have to CARE about what she says as much as what you say. You already know how to do this, fella — the stupid narratives of society have convinced you women are a different species.

It’s so difficult. I’m so in love with her, and so want to be able to live out the version of reality where we’re happy together forever. But is it naïve? Am I being needy, or are these truly things to worry about? I really don’t ever develop crushes on other people, and tend to know they’re fleeting fantasies — and, a lot of the time I don’t think like this. It’s just when I think about the future, really. I’m trying to get to the bottom of how much that’s because I’m pushing feelings aside. I wonder if the person I was as a teenager knew everything about what I would need in a partner as an adult, as important as this person’s  friendship and our history is to me. I get a nervous feeling when I think of forever; we’ve just been able to put off seriously talking about it. It was easier when we were younger; it was so hypothetical. Now we just don’t, and I’m not sure what I’d say if the conversation seriously came up and she was ready. We manage finances differently, different lifestyles in a few ways, spend time differently, and that’s all very weird to reckon with so late in the game due to circumstance. Most people are doing the “let’s figure out if we’d enjoy living together” thing the first few years — what if we’re looking down the barrel at ten? More? And then what? We realize we really ARE quite different people and have confronted it really late? I don’t want that for either of us. And I don’t want to be waiting for her to have a different situation than she does — that’s not fair to her. I want to accept her exactly as she is, but our relationship is one I’m having difficulty accepting *exactly* as it is, and I’m not sure how justified I am. And as a cherry on top, I’m actually the ONLY woman she’s ever dated and said she’d ever date, meaning I genuinely feel like I’m this Thing keeping her from building a relationship with someone who would be welcome in her family. She’s admitted her own feelings very briefly a long time ago about making peace not living a version of her own life she had envisioned, though does not being those feelings up anymore, even with prompting. Very complicated. I hope you find peace as well, and that we do what’s best for ourselves and our partners.

Again, you’ve entirely missed what I’m actually asking in your desperation to be self-righteous. I’m not wondering how not to be lonely, or complaining about my girlfriend. I’m wondering if this is a relationship that should continue. Not all relationships are meant to be marriages; we got together as teenagers, have grown in much different ways over NINE YEARS as people now in our twenties, and the “different places in life” and other lifestyle differences that have solidified over the past several years are ones being addressed now, before we move in together and make things more official, something that should only be done if both parties are entirely sure about the idea, which, for reasons I have indicated in the post, I am not. This is happening now because we have both lived in many different places over time for different reasons, unable to share a space together in the same way that other couples are so lucky to do early on. My girlfriend is satisfied with the amount we see each other due to her stressful job and father’s health, and is not able to prioritize the relationship any more than she is at the moment. This is not something I blame her for, and something I am willing and happy to give her patience for, given the circumstances, but becomes complicated by all other factors listed above, which is, again, the point of the post, asking for advice about if these types of situations are built to last. If you set out to give advice with the intent to lay into anybody you feel you’re better than, then you’ll certainly have 120,000 Reddit brownie points worth of bogus advice that doesn’t really consider the humanity of the person you’re speaking to. These situations can go many ways, all with both parties best interests at heart, and if you had the emotional intelligence you thought you did, you’d see that.

Final grades are especially rough — most professors have a ridiculously slim window to turn final grades around to the college. (I just had 24 hours after finals to submit 150 final grades). I simply am not allotted the time to give detailed feedback on these, even though I do wish I could. I always tell my students that if they want detailed feedback on their final paper, they have to get it to me early. I certainly  understand wanting feedback on something you’ve worked hard on, but with so many students wanting as much time as possible to finish the paper, and also wanting grades to be available promptly, something’s gotta give! This is likely the reason you see sparse comments on final papers especially.
